explanations.explanation: Infants, friend. Paul says he couldn't address them as spiritual, but as worldly, “…as infants in Christ.” I think that's a kind way to say there's growing left to do, and he still opens by calling them “Brothers.”
Elders would mean grown and seasoned, and Paul says the opposite. He calls them infants in Christ. I earned this tall chef's hat the slow way, and nobody hands that out on day one either.
Not strangers, friend. Paul calls them “Brothers” and says they are infants “in Christ.” Strangers wouldn't be in Him at all, and Paul's whole point is that they're in Him but still need to grow.

Close, but Paul says the opposite. He gave them milk because they weren't ready for solid food, and then he adds, “In fact, you are still not ready…” So the answer is False. Paul says they aren't ready even now.
Right, baker. Paul says, “…you are still not ready…” He gave milk then, and he says they're still in that spot. That's not an insult to me. It's a doctor reading the chart.

Jealousy is the word. Paul says, “…there is jealousy and dissension among you…” and that's why he calls them worldly. When people keep score over who has the better leader, jealousy is usually standing right behind them.
Greed is a sneaky one, but it's not the word Paul uses here. He says there is jealousy and dissension among them. Same family of trouble, different name on the box.
Paul doesn't call them lazy. The word is jealousy, and it comes with dissension. These folks had plenty of energy, and they were spending it on the wrong thing.

Mere men. Paul asks, “…are you not mere men?” When they said “I follow Paul” and “I follow Apollos,” they were acting on a very human level. He's not saying it to be harsh. He's pulling them back down to earth so they can look up again.
That's a nice title, but it's not what Paul says. After hearing “I follow Paul” and “I follow Apollos,” he asks, “…are you not mere men?” He doesn't hand out a gold star for picking teams.
Paul doesn't call them teachers at all here. His question is, “…are you not mere men?” The team talk had them sounding impressive, and Paul just let the air out of it.

Servants. Paul says Apollos and himself are “…servants through whom you believed…” and the Lord has assigned each one a role. That's it. Neither of them took the job, and neither of them owns the crowd.
Not quite. Paul says the Lord assigned each his role, so the church didn't pick them like a team captain. They are servants through whom the Corinthians believed.
Paul never calls himself or Apollos a judge here. He says they are servants, and the Lord assigned each his role. A servant doesn't sit on a throne, friend. A servant carries the tray.
Close, but flip it. Paul says, “I planted the seed and Apollos watered it…” That's two jobs, and neither one is making it grow. The answer is False.
Right. Paul planted, Apollos watered, “…but God made it grow.” The growing is God's part. Nobody with a watering can gets to take credit for the harvest.

True. Paul says the one who plants and the one who waters are “one in purpose.” They're not rival teams, they're on the same crew. The Corinthians were choosing sides, and Paul says there was only ever one side.
Paul says the opposite. The one who plants and the one who waters are “one in purpose.” They aren't rivals and they aren't competing. They're pulling the same direction.
Labor. Paul says each “…will be rewarded according to his own labor.” The reward follows the work, not the applause. I've pressed a lot of dough with nobody clapping, and that still counts.
Fame isn't the measure. Paul says each will be rewarded according to his own labor. A famous name and a faithful worker are two different things.
Funny pick, since followers were the whole argument in Corinth. But Paul says the reward is according to each one's own labor. Nobody gets paid by headcount.
God's field. Paul says, “…you are God's field, God's building.” After all that planting and watering, it fits. The Corinthians are the ground God is growing something in.
Flock is a picture Scripture uses in other places, but it's not the word here. Paul has been talking about planting and watering, so he says, “…you are God's field…” Stay with the farm, friend.
No army in this verse. Paul keeps to the garden and says, “…you are God's field, God's building.” After the shouting in Corinth, a quiet field sounds pretty nice.

Careful. Paul says, “But each one must be careful how he builds.” The foundation is already set, but what goes on top still matters. Measure twice, friend. I learned that the hard way with a cookie tray and a crooked rack.
Speed isn't the word. Paul says each one must be careful how he builds. A fast builder with sloppy work is just a fast way to a mess.
Boldness doesn't come up here. Paul says each one must be careful how he builds. Careful and bold can go together, but careful is the word he picks.

Jesus Christ. Paul says no one can lay any other foundation than the one already laid, “…which is Jesus Christ.” Everything else gets built on Him. It's not a team, it's not a favorite preacher. It's Him.
David, Israel's king (2 Samuel 5:3), is a big name in the Bible. But Paul says the foundation already laid is Jesus Christ. David doesn't need to be the foundation, and Paul never says he is.

Peter, one of Jesus' apostles (Matthew 10:2), is a great name, but he's not the foundation Paul points to. Paul says it is Jesus Christ. Considering the Corinthians were splitting over leaders, that's exactly the point.

Fire. Paul says the Day will bring each builder's work to light and, “It will be revealed with fire…” Then the fire proves the quality of each man's work. Fire doesn't take opinions, friend. It just shows what's there.
No flood in this passage. Paul says it will be revealed with fire. Water would be a whole different picture.
Paul doesn't mention an earthquake here. He says the work will be revealed with fire, and the fire proves its quality. One test, and it's a hot one.
True. Paul says, “If what he has built survives, he will receive a reward.” If the work stands up to the fire, the builder is rewarded. Good work lasts, and Paul says it's noticed.
Paul says the opposite. “If what he has built survives, he will receive a reward.” So the answer is True. Work that stands through the fire gets rewarded.

Careful with this one, baker. If the work burns up, the builder suffers loss, but Paul says, “He himself will be saved, but only as if through the flames.” So the answer is False. The work is lost, not the man.

Right. Paul says if it's burned up, he will suffer loss, but “He himself will be saved, but only as if through the flames.” That's a real loss, and I think it would sting. Still, the builder is saved.

Temple. Paul asks, “Do you not know that you yourselves are God's temple, and that God's Spirit dwells in you?” That's a big word to give people who were busy arguing. It tells them they're a place where God's Spirit lives.
Not a city. Paul says they are God's temple, and that God's Spirit dwells in them. A temple is a place where God dwells, and that's the point.
An altar isn't the word. Paul says, “…you yourselves are God's temple…” and he adds that God's Spirit dwells in them. The picture is a dwelling place.
Holy. Paul says, “…for God's temple is holy, and you are that temple.” That's why he took the warning before it so seriously. What belongs to God is not something to tear down.
Finished isn't what Paul says. He says God's temple is holy, and they are that temple. Even a work in progress can be holy.
Paul doesn't call it hidden. He says God's temple is holy, and the Corinthians are that temple. Nothing about it is a secret.

True, and it sounds backwards on purpose. Paul says, “…he should become a fool, so that he may become wise.” The worldly kind of wise has to let go first. I've been a fool plenty of times, friend, so I'm halfway there.

Paul really does say it. If anyone thinks he is wise in this age, “…he should become a fool, so that he may become wise.” So the answer is True. It sounds backwards, but it's right there in the verse.
Boasting in men. Paul says, “Therefore, stop boasting in men.” That's the whole fight in Corinth, one person bragging about their favorite leader. Paul says to quit it.
The Law doesn't come up in this part. Paul says, “Therefore, stop boasting in men.” The trouble here is bragging about people.
Courts aren't in this passage. Right after talking about worldly wisdom, Paul says, “Therefore, stop boasting in men.” That's the habit he wants dropped.
Christ. Paul says, “…and you belong to Christ, and Christ belongs to God.” They have everything, and they belong to Him. That's the right way around.
Paul is the one writing, and he says it isn't him. He lists himself among the things that belong to them. Then he says, “…you belong to Christ…”
Apollos is on the list of things that belong to the Corinthians, not the one they belong to. Paul says, “…you belong to Christ, and Christ belongs to God.” Nobody gets to put their name on that.
